parts.summary: Help campus students find study rooms using student-reported check-ins. Noor, Tom and Ilias will build a free web app and show it in a 3-minute live demo at hour 24.
parts.details:
The university PDF supplies room names and buildings, not live availability. Show reported check-in counts and “Counts refreshed at”. This time says when the server calculated the counts, not when a student last visited. Zero check-ins means “No recent check-ins — availability unknown”.

Copy a small, clearly labelled room sample from the PDF during the hackathon. Students can choose a room, tap “I’m here”, renew their visit and check out. Visits expire after 60 minutes.

Success means a student can report a visit quickly and another phone can see the change. The pitch connects this flow to less uncertainty when looking for study space. No AI is needed.

parts.summary: Build a phone-friendly list, check-in and checkout, automatic expiry, and a rehearsed live demo. Schedule 36 person-hours and preserve 16 hours for fixes.
parts.details:
Done means:
- The agreed PDF rooms appear with building names, reported counts and honest availability labels.
- Check-in appears on a second phone after refresh; checkout removes it. Repeat taps and retries of an uncertain request never create duplicates or extend a visit twice.
- Visits stop counting after 60 minutes. My check-in refreshes with room counts and shows an expired message with a check-in-again action.
- Initial loading never looks like zero reports. A failed refresh keeps old counts visibly marked stale, with their last successful refresh time.
- Failed actions never show success. An uncertain response asks the student to retry or refresh; success requires server confirmation.
- The public site uses HTTPS and Secure cookies. The laptop fallback works with two separate browser sessions on localhost, without requiring phone access.
- Noor completes a timed 3-minute pitch. A recording of the working flow is saved locally before hour 23.

Hour 2: agree room sample, wording and example requests and replies. Hour 6: deploy a small working page; room list and visit rules work separately. Hour 12: complete one visit flow across two phones. Hour 18: freeze all new features. Hours 18–22: test, fix and prepare the backup. Hours 22–24: finish recording before hour 23 and rehearse. Repeat the demo flow after any late fix.

Noor has 11 scheduled hours and 5 spare; Tom has 12 scheduled and 6 spare; Ilias has 13 scheduled and 5 spare. Technical demo setup, design review and architecture work are included in these allocations, not added to them.

Defer the map, notifications, university login and noise levels. If milestones slip, reduce polish and room coverage while keeping truthful labels and the complete visit flow.

parts.summary: Refresh room counts and the browser’s own visit together every 15 seconds while the page is visible. Use server-confirmed results for every action.
parts.details:
Use GET /api/rooms, GET /api/me, POST /api/check-in and POST /api/check-out. GET /api/rooms returns rooms with names, buildings and active counts, plus server_time and my_check_in. The latter is either null or {room_id, expires_at}. GET /api/me returns the same visit fields and server_time. Calculate a room-list response using one time value and a consistent database read.

The interface labels server_time “Counts refreshed at”. It is not a student activity timestamp. Poll the combined response every 15 seconds while visible, refresh when returning to the page, and refresh after each confirmed action. Keep old values visibly stale if refresh fails.

One browser can have one active visit. A new, deliberate check-in sets expiry to server time plus 60 minutes. Checking into the same room explicitly renews it; switching replaces the old visit in one database transaction, meaning the whole change succeeds or none does. Checkout removes it.

Each deliberate action gets a unique request ID. Retrying uses the same ID. Store an action receipt so repeating that request cannot add a visit, renew it twice or repeat a switch. Allow only one unresolved action in the interface at a time. After a retry, fetch current state rather than treating an old receipt as the current visit.

When the server returns no visit and the previously known expiry has passed, show “Your check-in expired” and “Check in again”. Otherwise show no active visit. At the known expiry time, remove the active confirmation and refresh; if offline, say the last known visit has expired and mark counts stale. Passive refresh never renews a visit.

Keep counting, expiry and validation in small pure functions: data goes in and results come out. Pass time into these functions. Keep database, clock and request handling outside them. Test the rules without a server, share helpers and keep files below about 400 lines.

parts.summary: Store room names, buildings and temporary anonymous visits. Counts describe reports, not available seats.
parts.details:
Noor verifies a small PDF sample; Ilias loads it as room seed data in the repository. Room records contain id, name and building. Visit records contain a hashed random browser token, room_id and expires_at. Make the token unique so one browser has one active room. Short-lived action receipts contain the token hash, request ID and result; retain them for the event and clear them after judging.

Keep the raw browser token in a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax cookie. Secure restricts transmission to HTTPS; HttpOnly keeps page scripts from reading it; SameSite limits cross-site sending. Validate the origin of action requests. Return only aggregate counts and that browser’s own visit.

Public mode always enables Secure cookies. A separate development setting may disable Secure only for the laptop’s localhost HTTP mode. Bind that fallback to the laptop itself; do not expose it over venue Wi-Fi. Test cookie persistence separately in hosted and local modes.

Collect no names, university IDs, GPS or movement history. Delete checked-out visits immediately. Ignore expired visits on every count and remove them during requests. Clear visits and action receipts after judging. Back up room data and code, not attendance. Empty visits after a reset are acceptable.

Avoid logging tokens or action bodies. Ilias checks the host’s access-log retention because those logs may contain IP addresses.

parts.summary: Build one friendly room-list page with an embedded My check-in panel. Noor defines it in three Figma hours; Tom implements it within his existing frontend hours.
parts.details:
Group room cards by building. Each card shows its room name, reported count and “I’m here”. Put room information directly in the card. Keep My check-in near the top, showing the current room, expiry time, “Renew for 60 minutes” and “Check out”. This removes separate room-details navigation.

Use “3 reported check-ins” or “No recent check-ins — availability unknown”. Explain that counts are not seats left. Label the server timestamp “Counts refreshed at”. Remove “latest activity”: refreshing counts is not evidence of a recent student visit.

Before the first response, show “Loading rooms”, never zero counts. If refresh fails, keep the previous values with “Could not refresh — showing older counts” and the last successful refresh time. Offer Retry. If there are no previous values, show an error without invented counts.

While an action is pending, disable conflicting actions and show “Checking in…” or “Checking out…”. Confirm success only after the server accepts it. A timeout says “Could not confirm the change”; offer a retry using the same request ID. Do not make a new visit request for a retry.

Refresh My check-in with room counts. Show the server-provided expiry time. When the visit expires, show “Your check-in expired” and “Check in again”. If offline at expiry, say the last known visit has expired and keep counts marked stale. Reading or refreshing never renews a visit.

Use a light background, dark text, one warm accent and words beside status icons. Use at least 16px body text, strong contrast, visible keyboard focus and large touch buttons. Announce action results to screen readers. Avoid motion and custom illustrations.

Reuse the header, room card, visit panel and message box. Noor agrees wording with Ilias during her existing content task. Her three design hours define the layout and states. Tom’s four presentation hours implement the shared layout; his five integration hours connect its behavior. Noor’s two review hours are included in her six demo hours. All work uses free tools during the event, within the 36 scheduled hours and 16-hour reserve.

risks.action: Keep limits visible in app and pitch.
Agree examples by hour 2; complete flow by 12.

risks.risk: Forgotten or false visits distort counts.
risks.action: Expire visits; allow one per browser. Separate browsers can still submit false reports.
Deploy early; rehearse laptop and recording backups.

decision.title: What room status can we honestly show?

options.name: Recent student reports
options.good: Uses check-ins and makes missing information visible.
options.bad: Cannot confirm that a room is empty or full.
options.fit: Uses data the team can collect within 24 hours.

options.name: Verified free/busy status
options.good: Would directly answer whether space is available.
options.bad: Requires reliable occupancy or booking information.
options.fit: The team does not have the required data.

decision.why: Counts and clear limits give students useful evidence without promising a free seat.
decision.disagreement: The requested free/busy status cannot be established from the PDF and voluntary check-ins.

decision.title: List or map for day one?

options.name: Room list
options.good: Quick to build and scan on a phone.
options.bad: Does not show walking directions.
options.fit: Uses the PDF and preserves Tom’s implementation time.

options.name: Campus map
options.good: Helps students locate unfamiliar buildings.
options.bad: Needs verified locations and extra interaction work.
options.fit: Too uncertain for Tom’s 18 hours.

decision.why: Building names already exist in the PDF. Reliable check-ins matter more for this demo.

decision.title: App and storage

options.name: Flask, React and SQLite together
options.good: Uses both developers’ skills with one deployment.
options.bad: Needs a React build step and agreed response fields.
options.fit: Fits Tom and Ilias’s skills and existing task allocations.

options.name: Flask templates and plain JavaScript
options.good: Removes the React build step.
options.bad: Changes Tom’s familiar workflow.
options.fit: A possible simplification if React setup becomes a blocker.

options.name: Separate frontend and managed database
options.good: Can scale separately later.
options.bad: Adds accounts, settings and failure points.
options.fit: Too much setup for this free, 24-hour entry.

decision.why: It uses existing skills and keeps deployment small.

decision.title: Visit lifetime

options.name: 60 minutes with explicit renewal
options.good: Limits forgotten visits without frequent interruptions.
options.bad: A departed student can still count for up to an hour.
options.fit: A simple starting rule that Ilias can test and Noor can explain.

options.name: 30 minutes with explicit renewal
options.good: Removes forgotten visits sooner.
options.bad: Requires more frequent renewal during study.
options.fit: Equally buildable, but adds more interruptions.

decision.why: Use one clear rule for the demo and show its expiry in My check-in.

decision.title: Show the working flow live, with a recording ready

options.name: Live demo with recorded backup
options.good: Shows real changes and protects the presentation from failures.
options.bad: Requires rehearsed switching and reset.
options.fit: A narrow flow fits the developers’ allocations and Noor’s six demo hours.

options.name: Recording as the main demo
options.good: Predictable timing.
options.bad: Does not meet the live-demo requirement by itself.
options.fit: Useful only as the fallback for this brief.

decision.why: Live check-in and checkout demonstrate technical execution. A recording preserves evidence if the live setup fails.

decision.title: Live demo fallback

options.name: Laptop localhost with two browser sessions
options.good: Works without venue internet or phone networking.
options.bad: Does not demonstrate two physical phones.
options.fit: Fits the existing setup and verification hours.

options.name: Phones connected to a laptop server
options.good: Preserves the two-phone demonstration.
options.bad: Adds network access and local HTTPS setup.
options.fit: Too uncertain for this fallback budget.

decision.picked: Laptop localhost with two browser sessions
decision.why: The public app gets phone testing; the fallback proves shared state on a predictable connection.

decision.title: What room status means

options.name: Reported counts with unknown availability
options.good: Provides evidence without inventing occupancy.
options.bad: Cannot promise a seat.
options.fit: Works with voluntary reports and the PDF.

options.name: Inferred free/busy labels
options.good: Easy to scan.
options.bad: Missing reports can falsely imply an empty room.
options.fit: Unsupported by the available data.

decision.why: Show reported activity and count refresh time, while explaining that bookings and unreported occupants are unknown.
decision.disagreement: The requested free/busy status cannot be established from the supplied information.

decision.title: Start with a building-grouped list

options.name: Building-grouped list
options.good: Quick to scan and needs only names and buildings.
options.bad: Does not show walking directions.
options.fit: Uses the PDF and keeps Tom’s work small.

options.name: Campus map
options.good: Helps students compare locations.
options.bad: Needs verified coordinates and more interaction work.
options.fit: Risks the 24-hour deadline.

decision.why: It works on phones and during the three-minute demo using the available data.

decision.title: Keep the visit flow on one page

options.name: Room cards and embedded My check-in
options.good: Keeps actions visible and reduces navigation.
options.bad: Leaves less space for future room information.
options.fit: Fits Noor’s three design hours and Tom’s existing frontend allocation.

options.name: Separate Rooms, Details and My check-in views
options.good: Provides room for richer information later.
options.bad: Adds navigation and more states to design and test.
options.fit: Unnecessary for names, buildings and check-ins at this deadline.

decision.picked: Room cards and embedded My check-in
decision.why: The available room information fits on cards, and the active visit stays easy to find.

decision.title: Show reports with count refresh time

options.name: Reported counts with refresh time
options.good: Shows useful evidence and makes stale data visible.
options.bad: Cannot guarantee available seats or show when students last acted.
options.fit: Uses the agreed server response without adding data fields.

options.name: Binary free/busy labels
options.good: Easy to scan.
options.bad: Suggests knowledge of occupancy that the app lacks.
options.fit: Unsupported by the PDF and voluntary reports.

decision.why: Use the same honest labels in the app and pitch. “Counts refreshed at” describes the timestamp accurately.
decision.disagreement: The requested free/busy and filling-up claims imply information the team does not have.
